items.stem: Which part of a plant takes in water and mineral salts from the soil?
options: The stem
The leaves
The roots
The flowers

explain.why: The stem carries water and mineral salts up the plant, but it is the roots that take them in from the soil.
Leaves make food. They do not take in water and mineral salts from the soil.
Flowers help the plant make seeds. They are not in the soil and do not absorb water from it.

solution: The roots grow in the soil and take in water and mineral salts.

figure.alt: A potted plant in line art.

items.stem: Which part of a plant makes food for the plant?
options: The roots under the ground
The stem
The seeds inside the fruit
The leaves

explain.why: The roots are underground, where there is no sunlight. They absorb water and mineral salts; they do not make food.
The stem supports the plant and carries water and food. The leaves make the food.
Seeds can grow into new plants. They are not the part that makes food for the plant.

solution: Leaves use sunlight, water and carbon dioxide to make food.

figure.alt: A potted plant in line art.

items.stem: What is the main job of the stem of a plant?
options: To hold up the plant and carry water
To make food for the whole plant from sunlight
To take in water from the soil
To make new seeds for the plant

explain.why: Making food is the job of the leaves, not the stem.
The roots take in water from the soil. The stem only carries it upwards.
Seeds are made by the flower, not the stem.

solution: The stem holds the leaves and flowers up and carries water and food around the plant.

figure.alt: A potted plant in line art.

items.stem: Look at the picture of the potted plant. Which part holds the plant firmly in the soil?
options: Part A
Part B
Part D
Part C

explain.why: Part A is the flower. It helps the plant make seeds and does not hold the plant in the soil.
Part B is a leaf. It makes food and does not hold the plant in the soil.
Part C is the stem. It holds the plant up, but the roots are what grip the soil.

solution: The roots (part D) spread through the soil and hold the plant firmly in place.

figure.alt: A potted plant drawn in line art with its flower, a broad leaf, a stem and roots shown under the soil, with four marked positions.

items.stem: The picture shows a young bean plant. Part A is the first part to grow out of the seed and it grows down into the soil. What is part A?
options: A stem
A leaf
A root
A flower

explain.why: The stem grows upwards, carrying the leaves towards the light, not down into the soil.
Leaves grow in the air above the stem. Part A grows down into the soil.
A flower only appears later, once the plant is grown.

solution: The first part out of a germinating seed grows down as the root, to take in water.

figure.alt: A young bean seedling in line art.

items.stem: Adam put a cutting from a money plant into a bottle of water. After two weeks, new parts grew from the stem into the water. What are these new parts?
options: Leaves
Roots
Flowers
Fruits

explain.why: Leaves grow in the air, where they get sunlight, not in the water.
Flowers need a grown plant and are not what grows into the water.
Fruits grow from flowers and not from the stem into the water.

solution: Roots grew from the stem so the cutting could take in water.

items.stem: Kangkong grows in water and wet soil. Which part of the kangkong plant makes food for it?
options: The roots
The hollow stem
The water around it
The leaves

explain.why: The roots take in water and mineral salts. They do not make food.
The stem carries water and food; the leaves make the food.
Water is one of the things the leaves use, but water is not a part of the plant.

solution: The leaves of kangkong make the food for the plant.

figure.alt: A kangkong plant floating in water.

items.stem: When we eat carrot, which part of the carrot plant are we eating?
options: A stem
A root
A leaf
A fruit

explain.why: A stem is the part that holds up a plant. The orange carrot is not a stem.
The leaves of a carrot plant are the green, feathery parts above the ground.
A fruit holds seeds and grows from a flower. A carrot grows under the soil.

solution: The orange part of a carrot is a thick root that stores food.

items.stem: Which of these foods is the leaf of a plant?
options: Carrot
Cucumber
Sugar cane
Cabbage

explain.why: A carrot is a root.
A cucumber is a fruit; it has seeds inside.
Sugar cane is the stem of the plant.

solution: Cabbage is made of leaves.

figure.alt: A potted plant in line art.

items.stem: A rain tree in a Singapore park is very tall. Which part holds its leaves up so they can get sunlight?
options: The trunk, which is its stem
The roots under the ground
The flowers on its branches
The fruits hanging from its branches

explain.why: The roots hold the tree firmly in the soil, but it is the stem that lifts the leaves.
Flowers help make seeds. They do not hold leaves up.
Fruits protect seeds. They do not hold leaves up.

solution: The trunk is the stem of the tree and keeps the leaves up in the light.

items.stem: Look at the picture of the potted plant. What does part C do for the plant?
options: It takes in water and mineral salts from the soil
It makes food for the plant
It makes the seeds for the plant
It holds up the leaves and flower

explain.why: Taking in water is done by the roots (part D), not the stem.
Food is made by the leaf (part B), not the stem.
Seeds are made by the flower (part A), not the stem.

solution: Part C is the stem. It holds up the leaves and the flower.

figure.alt: A potted plant drawn in line art with its flower, a broad leaf, a stem and roots shown under the soil, with four marked positions.

items.stem: Look at the picture of the potted plant. What is the main job of part B?
options: To hold the plant in the soil
To make food for the plant using light
To carry water up the plant
To make seeds

explain.why: Holding the plant in the soil is the job of the roots (part D).
Carrying water up is the job of the stem (part C).
Seeds are made by the flower (part A).

solution: Part B is a leaf. Leaves make food for the plant.

figure.alt: A potted plant drawn in line art with its flower, a broad leaf, a stem and roots shown under the soil, with four marked positions.

items.stem: Where do most plants get the water they need?
options: From the air, through the flowers
From the soil, taken in through the roots
From the soil, through the leaves
From sunlight, through the stem

explain.why: Flowers do not take in water for the plant.
The water comes from the soil but it enters through the roots, not the leaves.
Sunlight is energy for making food. It is not a source of water.

solution: Roots take in water from the soil.

figure.alt: A potted plant in line art.

items.stem: Which sentence about the roots of a plant is correct?
options: They hold the plant firmly in the soil.
They make food for the plant using sunlight.
They carry seeds to new places.
They are always found above the ground.

explain.why: Food is made by the leaves. Roots in the soil get no sunlight.
Roots do not carry seeds. Seeds are spread by wind, water or animals.
Most roots grow in the soil, under the ground.

solution: Roots grip the soil and hold the plant firmly.

figure.alt: A potted plant in line art.

items.stem: Which of these does a plant need to make its own food?
options: Sunlight, oxygen and soil
Water, oxygen and mineral salts from the soil
Sunlight, water and carbon dioxide
Sunlight, oxygen and mineral salts

explain.why: A plant needs carbon dioxide and water to make food. Oxygen and soil are not what it makes food from.
Without sunlight and carbon dioxide a plant cannot make food, and oxygen is not needed for making it.
Food is made from carbon dioxide and water. Oxygen and mineral salts are not the materials.

solution: Leaves use sunlight, water and carbon dioxide to make food.

items.stem: The stem carries water from the roots up to the ____.
options: leaves
roots of the plant
soil around the roots
air around the plant

explain.why: Water goes up from the roots through the stem. It does not carry it down into the roots.
Water is taken in from the soil; it is not carried to the soil.
Water is carried to the leaves. Only a little leaves the plant, as water vapour.

solution: Water goes from the roots, up the stem, to the leaves.

items.stem: A strong wind blows across a garden. Which part helps a plant stay in the ground?
options: The leaves
The flowers
The roots
The fruits

explain.why: Leaves make food. A strong wind may even tear them.
Flowers help the plant make seeds. They do not hold it in the ground.
Fruits protect seeds. They do not hold the plant in the ground.

solution: Roots grip the soil and hold the plant firmly.

figure.alt: A potted plant in line art.

items.stem: In the picture, which letter shows the part that takes in water from the soil?
options: Part P
Part R
Part S
Part Q

explain.why: Part P is the stem. It carries water up but does not take it in from the soil.
Part R is the flower. It helps the plant make seeds.
Part S is a leaf. Leaves make food and do not take in water from the soil.

solution: Part Q is the roots, under the soil. They take in water.

items.stem: Look at the picture of the orchid growing on a tree. Part B hangs in the air. What is part B?
options: Stems
Leaves
Roots
Fruits

explain.why: Stems hold up leaves and flowers. These long hanging parts are roots.
The orchid's leaves are the flat green parts, not the long hanging parts.
Fruits hold seeds and grow from flowers. These hanging parts are not fruits.

solution: Part B is a group of aerial roots hanging in the air.

figure.alt: An orchid growing on a tree trunk in line art.

items.stem: Look at the picture of the potted plant. Which statement about parts B and C is correct?
options: Part C makes food; part B carries the water up to it
Part B makes food; part C carries water to it
Part B makes food; part D carries water to it
Part A makes food; part C carries water to it

explain.why: The roles are swapped. The leaf (part B) makes food and the stem (part C) carries water.
Part D, the roots, takes water in, but it is the stem (part C) that carries the water up to the leaf.
Part A is the flower, which makes seeds. Food is made by the leaf.

solution: Part B is a leaf and it makes the food.
Part C is the stem and it carries water up to the leaf.

figure.alt: A potted plant drawn in line art with its flower, a broad leaf, a stem and roots shown under the soil, with four marked positions.

items.stem: Dad forgot to water the pot plant for a week. The leaves now droop. Why?
options: The leaves could not take in water from the air
The stem stopped carrying food to the leaves
The roots could not take in enough water
The flowers used up all the water in the plant

explain.why: Leaves do not take in water for the plant. The roots do.
The stem still carries food. The problem is that there is too little water to carry.
Flowers do not use up the water. The soil had little water for the roots to take in.

solution: Roots can only take in water from the soil.
With dry soil, the leaves lose water and droop.

items.stem: Which statement about stomata is correct?
options: They are tiny openings on the roots that let water and mineral salts in
They are tiny tubes in the stem that carry food around
They are tiny openings under the leaf for gases and water vapour
They are tiny openings on petals that let insects in

explain.why: Roots take in water through root hairs. Stomata are on leaves.
Tubes in the stem carry water and food, but they are not stomata.
Stomata are far too small for insects and are found on leaves.

solution: Stomata are tiny openings on a leaf. Gases and water vapour move in and out through them.

items.stem: Mr Lim moves a small plant from one pot to another. Why does he keep the soil around its roots?
options: So that the leaves can take in more sunlight
So that the stem can make food in the soil
So that he does not damage the roots
So that the flowers will open sooner

explain.why: Soil around the roots does not change how much light the leaves get.
The stem does not make food, and it is not inside the soil.
Soil around the roots does not make flowers open sooner.

solution: Roots take in water and mineral salts.
Keeping the soil on them stops them being damaged.

items.stem: A plant is kept in a dark cupboard for two weeks. Its leaves turn pale and yellow. Why?
options: The roots could not take in any air
The stem carried too much water to the leaves
The flowers took all the food
The leaves cannot make food without light

explain.why: Roots take in water and mineral salts. Lack of light is the problem here.
Too much water in the stem is not the cause. The leaves need light to make food.
Flowers do not take all the food. The leaves are unable to make it in the dark.

solution: Leaves need sunlight to make food.
In the dark they cannot, and they turn yellow.

items.stem: Which part of a plant carries the food made in the leaves to the other parts?
options: The stem
The roots
The petals
The seeds

explain.why: The roots take in water and mineral salts. Food is carried by the stem.
Petals attract insects and do not carry food.
Seeds grow into new plants and do not carry food.

solution: The stem has tubes that carry food from the leaves to the other parts.

items.stem: Which job is done by both the roots and the stem?
options: Making food for the plant
Making seeds for the plant
Helping to keep the plant upright
Taking in carbon dioxide for the plant

explain.why: Only the leaves make food.
Only the flower makes seeds.
Carbon dioxide enters through tiny openings in the leaves.

solution: Roots hold the plant in the soil and the stem holds it up, so both help it stay upright.

items.stem: Which row matches each plant part with its job correctly?
options: Root: takes in water; leaf: makes food
Root: makes food; leaf: takes in water
Stem: takes in water; flower: holds the plant up
Leaf: makes seeds; stem: makes food

explain.why: The jobs are swapped. Roots take in water and leaves make food.
Roots take in water and the stem holds the plant up. Flowers make seeds.
Flowers make seeds and leaves make food. The stem does neither.

solution: Roots take in water. Leaves make food.

items.stem: Which row gives a correct job for each of the parts named?
options: Stem: carries water up; flower: makes the seeds
Stem: makes seeds; flower: carries water
Root: carries water; leaf: makes seeds
Leaf: holds the plant up; root: makes food

explain.why: The jobs are swapped. Flowers make seeds and the stem carries water.
Roots take in water, and seeds are made by flowers, not leaves.
The stem holds the plant up, and food is made by leaves, not roots.

solution: The stem carries water. The flower makes seeds.

items.stem: In the picture, which letter shows the part that carries water from the roots to the leaves?
options: Part P
Part Q
Part S
Part R

explain.why: Part P is the flower. It helps the plant make seeds.
Part Q is the roots. They take in water but do not carry it all the way to the leaves.
Part R is a leaf. Water arrives there; the leaf does not carry it from the roots.

solution: Part S is the stem. It carries water from the roots up to the leaves.

items.stem: The leaf of the chilli plant (part C) is wide and thin. How does its shape help the plant?
options: It can store a lot of water for the dry times
It can hold the plant firmly in the soil
It can attract bees to the plant
It can catch a lot of sunlight to make food for the plant

explain.why: Storing water is what a cactus stem does, not a wide, thin leaf.
Holding the plant in the soil is done by the roots.
Bees are attracted to flowers (part A), not leaves.

solution: A wide, thin leaf has a large surface that catches more sunlight to make food.

figure.alt: A chilli plant in line art with a flower, a ripe chilli with seeds showing, a leaf and a stem, with four marked positions.

items.stem: Tall trees such as the angsana have thick, strong trunks. Why do they need them?
options: To take in water from the soil
To hold up the heavy branches and leaves
To make food for the whole tree from sunlight
To hold the seeds of the tree

explain.why: The roots take in water from the soil, not the trunk.
Food is made in the leaves, not the trunk.
Seeds are made by flowers and held in fruits, not in the trunk.

solution: The trunk is the stem. A thick one can hold up many heavy branches and leaves.

items.stem: The picture shows a bean seedling. Part C, the first leaves, will start to do an important job. What is it?
options: Taking in water and minerals from the soil
Holding the plant in the soil
Making the seeds
Making food for the young plant

explain.why: Water is taken in by the root (part A), not by the leaves.
Holding the plant in the soil is done by the root.
Seeds are made by flowers, not by the first leaves.

solution: The first leaves use sunlight, water and carbon dioxide to make food.

figure.alt: A young bean seedling in line art.

items.stem: Which of these lists has only roots that people eat?
options: Carrot and sugar cane
Carrot and sweet potato
Spinach and sweet potato
Cabbage and cucumber

explain.why: Sugar cane is a stem, not a root.
Spinach is a leaf, not a root.
Cabbage is made of leaves and a cucumber is a fruit.

solution: Carrot and sweet potato are thick roots that store food.

items.stem: Two similar plants, P and Q, are each put in a clear plastic bag as shown. Plant P has all its leaves and plant Q has all its leaves removed. Both are placed in the sun for one day. In which bag will more water droplets form, and why?
options: Plant Q, because its stem takes in more water
Plant P, because its leaves lose water vapour
Plant P, because its roots make water for the leaves
Both the same, because the stems lose equal water

explain.why: Without leaves, plant Q loses much less water vapour, so fewer droplets form.
Roots take in water; they do not make it. The droplets come from water vapour lost by the leaves.
Most water vapour is lost through the leaves, so the plant with leaves loses more.

solution: Water vapour escapes mainly from the leaves.
Plant P has leaves, so more water vapour collects in its bag.

options: Without roots it could not take in water
Without leaves it could not make enough food
Without a stem it could not hold itself up and carry water
Without sunlight it grew more slowly

explain.why: Plant Q still had its roots. Only its leaves were removed.
Plant Q still had its stem. Only its leaves were removed.
Both plants had the same sunlight. The only change was the leaves.

solution: P and Q differ only in having leaves.
Without leaves, Q could not make food, so it grew very little.

items.stem: In the experiment in the table, why were P and Q given the same soil, water and sunlight?
options: So the leaves are the only thing that is different
So that both plants grow to the same height
So that the roots make more food in both
So that Q can grow new leaves much faster than P

explain.why: The aim is to see if the leaves make a difference, so the heights can differ.
Roots do not make food. The conditions are kept the same to make the test fair.
The aim is not to help Q. It is to keep every other condition the same.

solution: A fair test changes one thing only.
Here that is whether the plant has leaves.

items.stem: Look at the picture of the potted plant. Mei Ling cuts through part C just above the soil, but leaves the pot in the sun. What happens to the leaves?
options: They wilt because water cannot reach them
They stay the same because the roots still supply water
They grow bigger because they get more sunlight
They turn into fruits

explain.why: The roots are still in the soil but the cut stem can no longer carry water up to the leaves.
More sunlight is not the result of a cut stem. The leaves are cut off from water.
Leaves do not turn into fruits. Fruits grow from flowers.

solution: Part C is the stem. It carries water up to the leaves.
Once it is cut, the water cannot get to them and they wilt.

figure.alt: A potted plant drawn in line art with its flower, a broad leaf, a stem and roots shown under the soil, with four marked positions.

items.stem: Look at the picture of the potted plant. If all of part B were removed, what would the plant be unable to do for itself?
options: Take in water and mineral salts from soil
Make enough food to stay healthy
Hold itself in the soil
Carry water up the plant

explain.why: Water and mineral salts are taken in by the roots (part D), which are still there.
The roots (part D) still hold the plant in the soil.
The stem (part C) is still there to carry water.

solution: Part B is the leaf, which makes food for the plant.
Without it the plant cannot make enough food.

figure.alt: A potted plant drawn in line art with its flower, a broad leaf, a stem and roots shown under the soil, with four marked positions.

items.stem: Ravi wants to find out if a leaf needs light to make food. Which is the fairest way?
options: Cover one leaf of plant A with foil and leave all of plant B uncovered
Cover the whole plant with foil at night and uncover it in the day
Cover one leaf with foil, leave another leaf on the same plant uncovered
Keep one plant in a cupboard and another kind of plant in the sun

explain.why: Two different plants may differ in other ways. Use two leaves of the same plant.
The leaf is only in the dark at night anyway, so there is nothing to compare.
The two plants are different kinds, so the plant type is changed as well as light.

solution: Use two leaves on the same plant and change only the light.
One is covered with foil. The other is not.

items.stem: Which set-up is the fairest way to find out if leaves cause water loss?
options: Two plants of different kinds, one with leaves removed, in bags
Two similar plants, one with leaves removed, one in a bag and the other without a bag
Two similar plants, one in the sun and one in the dark, in bags
Two similar plants in same pots, one with leaves removed, both bagged

explain.why: The plants differ in kind, so you cannot tell if the leaves caused the difference.
Only one has a bag, so the bag is changed too.
This tests light, not leaves.

solution: Change only the leaves.
Everything else, such as plant, pot, bag and place, stays the same.

items.stem: A leaf is covered on its underside with petroleum jelly, which blocks the stomata. What will happen?
options: The leaf takes in more water from the wet soil
The leaf takes in more sunlight and so makes more food
The leaf takes in less carbon dioxide and makes less food
The leaf turns into a flower

explain.why: Water comes from the roots, not the leaf, and blocked stomata would not change that.
Jelly on the underside does not give the leaf more sunlight.
A leaf never turns into a flower. Blocked stomata cut the supply of carbon dioxide.

solution: Stomata let carbon dioxide into the leaf.
With them blocked, the leaf makes less food.

items.stem: A white flower is placed in red-coloured water. After a few hours, its petals have red lines. What does this show?
options: The flower takes in water through its petals
The stem carries water up to the flower
The roots make red water for the flower
The leaves make red food for the flower

explain.why: The coloured water travelled up from the cut end of the stem and was not absorbed through the petals.
Roots take in water; they do not make colour.
The red colour came from the water the stem carried up.

solution: The coloured water moved up the stem to the petals.

items.stem: A money plant cutting has no roots. After two weeks in water, roots grow from the stem. What can the cutting now do?
options: Make food in its new roots
Make seeds in its new roots
Carry water in its new roots up to the leaves
Take in water and mineral salts to grow

explain.why: Food is made by the leaves, not the roots.
Seeds are made by flowers, not by the roots.
The roots take water in; the stem carries it up.

solution: The new roots can take in water and mineral salts, so the cutting can grow.

items.stem: Mrs Tan repots a plant and cuts off most of its roots. Even with wet soil, the plant wilts. Why?
options: The leaves can no longer make any food in the wet soil
The stem has to take in water instead
The few roots left cannot take in enough water
The flowers take too much water

explain.why: Leaves do not work in the soil. They make food above the ground.
The stem does not take in water from the soil.
The flowers are not the cause. The few roots left cannot supply enough water.

solution: Roots take in the water.
With most roots cut off, not enough water reaches the leaves.

items.stem: Carrot leaves are removed every week while the plant grows. The carrot roots stay very small. Why?
options: The roots take in less water without leaves
The stem pushes food out of the root
Less food is made, so less is stored
The root gets too much sunlight without leaves

explain.why: The roots can still take in water; the main change is that less food is made.
The stem carries food to the root. It does not take it out.
The root grows under the soil, where there is no sunlight.

solution: Leaves make the food that is stored in the carrot root.
Without leaves, little food is made to store.

items.stem: Which shows the path taken by water in a plant?
options: Soil, stem, roots, leaves, then air
Soil, roots, stem, leaves, air
Soil, leaves, stem, roots, air
Air, leaves, stem, roots, soil

explain.why: Water is taken in by the roots before it moves up the stem.
Water does not enter through the leaves. The roots take it in.
This is the opposite way. Water goes from the soil, up through the plant, and out as vapour.

solution: Roots take water from the soil. It goes up the stem to the leaves, and leaves as water vapour.

items.stem: Hui says, "A plant does not need roots if its leaves get lots of sunlight." Which reply is the best?
options: Roots are needed to make food from sunlight
Roots are needed for the leaves to take in carbon dioxide
Roots are needed to give the plant sunlight
Without roots the leaves would lack the water that they need to make food

explain.why: Roots do not make food. Leaves do.
Leaves take in carbon dioxide through their stomata.
Roots do not give a plant sunlight. They take in water.

solution: Leaves need water as well as sunlight to make food.
The roots take in the water.

items.stem: A gardener ties a tall plant to a stick so that it does not fall over. Which part of the plant is held up by the stick?
options: The stem
The roots
The flower only
The seeds

explain.why: The roots are under the soil. The stick holds up the part above the soil.
The stick holds up the whole plant, not just the flower.
Seeds form inside the fruit. They are not what holds a plant up.

solution: The stem holds up the leaves and flowers, so the stick helps the stem.

items.stem: Hui plants a bean seed in wet soil. Which part of the young plant first grows down into the soil?
options: The first leaves
The flower
The fruit
The root

explain.why: The first leaves grow upwards into the light, not down into the soil.
The flower grows much later, on an adult plant.
The fruit forms after the flower. It is not the first part to grow.

solution: A young plant grows its root down first to take in water and hold itself in the soil.

figure.alt: A bean seed cut open, showing its outer covering and the parts inside.

items.stem: Which part of a plant is usually found under the soil?
options: The leaves
The flowers
The roots
The fruits

explain.why: Leaves grow above the soil where they can get light.
Flowers grow above the soil, where insects can reach them.
Fruits grow above the soil on the plant.

solution: Roots grow down in the soil. The leaves, flowers and fruits are above it.

items.stem: Which part of a plant joins the roots to the leaves?
options: The flower
The stem
The fruit
The seed

explain.why: The flower is at the top of the plant and does not join the roots to the leaves.
A fruit holds seeds. It is not a link between roots and leaves.
A seed grows into a new plant. It does not join parts of the plant.

solution: The stem is the part between the roots and the leaves.

figure.alt: A potted plant in line art.

items.stem: Which part of a healthy plant is usually green?
options: The leaves
The roots
The petals
The seeds

explain.why: Roots are under the soil, away from light, and are usually pale or brown.
Petals are usually brightly coloured to attract insects, not green.
Seeds are usually brown or another colour inside a fruit, not green like leaves.

solution: Leaves are green because they hold the green substance that helps them make food.

figure.alt: A potted plant in line art.

items.stem: Look at the picture of the potted plant. Mei Ling picks off part A every day. What will the plant be unable to make?
options: Food
Roots
Seeds
Water

explain.why: Food is made in the leaves (part B), which are still there.
Roots grow from the plant under the soil. They do not come from the flower.
A plant does not make water. It takes water in through its roots.

solution: Part A is the flower. Flowers make the seeds.
With no flowers there will be no seeds.

figure.alt: A potted plant drawn in line art with its flower, a broad leaf, a stem and roots shown under the soil, with four marked positions.

items.stem: Look at the picture of the potted plant. Water must travel from the soil to the leaves. Which shows the parts it passes through, in order?
options: B, C, D
D, C, B
D, B, C
C, D, B

explain.why: This is the wrong way round. Water moves up, from the roots to the leaves.
The water cannot jump from the roots to the leaves. It goes up the stem first.
Water enters at the roots (D), not at the stem.

solution: Part D is the roots, part C is the stem and part B is a leaf.
Water goes in at the roots, up the stem and into the leaves.

figure.alt: A potted plant drawn in line art with its flower, a broad leaf, a stem and roots shown under the soil, with four marked positions.

items.stem: Look at the picture of the potted plant. Part D is torn off when the plant is pulled out of the soil. After some days the leaves droop. Why?
options: The plant cannot take in enough water
The plant cannot make seeds
The stem cannot hold up the plant
The leaves cannot get any sunlight

explain.why: Seeds do not affect the leaves drooping. The leaves droop because of too little water.
The stem is still there. Drooping comes from a lack of water.
The leaves are still in the light. The problem is below the soil.

solution: Part D is the roots, which take in water.
Without roots the plant cannot take in enough water, so the leaves droop.

figure.alt: A potted plant drawn in line art with its flower, a broad leaf, a stem and roots shown under the soil, with four marked positions.

items.stem: Which of these is NOT a job of the roots of a plant?
options: Holding the plant in the soil
Taking in water from the soil
Taking in mineral salts from the soil
Making food for the plant

explain.why: This is a job of the roots, so it is not the answer.
This is a job of the roots, so it is not the answer.
This is a job of the roots, so it is not the answer.

solution: Roots hold the plant and take in water and mineral salts.
Food is made in the leaves, not in the roots.

figure.alt: A potted plant in line art.

items.stem: Aisha cuts the stem of a potted plant just above the soil and leaves the top part in the pot. After a few days the leaves dry up. Why?
options: The leaves cannot make seeds any more
The roots cannot hold the plant firmly
Water from the roots cannot reach the leaves
The leaves take in too much sunlight

explain.why: Leaves do not make seeds. They dry up because they get no water.
The roots are still in the soil. The cut stem breaks the path for water.
Light was the same as before. The change is the cut stem.

solution: The stem carries water from the roots up to the leaves.
When the stem is cut, no water can reach the leaves, so they dry up.

figure.alt: A potted plant in line art.

items.stem: Sugar cane juice comes from the tall, thick stalks of the sugar cane plant. Which part of the plant is the stalk?
options: The stem
The root
The leaf
The fruit

explain.why: Roots grow under the soil. The tall stalk is above it.
Leaves are the thin green blades. The thick stalk is not a leaf.
A fruit holds seeds. The stalk is the part that holds the plant up.

solution: The tall, thick part that holds up the leaves is the stem.

items.stem: We eat the green heads of broccoli. These heads are bunches of buds that have not opened. Which part of the broccoli plant do we eat?
options: The roots
The leaves
The seeds
The flowers

explain.why: The heads are above the ground. Roots are under the soil.
The heads are buds that would open into flowers. They are not leaves.
The buds have not made seeds yet.

solution: The heads are flower buds, so we eat the flowers of the plant.

items.stem: A sheet of plastic covers the soil of a potted plant. Water is poured only onto the plastic. After a few days the leaves droop. What is the reason?
options: The leaves cannot make food without plastic
The stem has too much water
Water cannot reach the roots in the soil
The flowers are using all the water

explain.why: Plastic has nothing to do with making food. The soil is blocked so the roots cannot get water.
The stem is getting less water, not more.
Flowers do not use up the water. The roots simply cannot reach any.

solution: Plants take in water through the roots in the soil.
The plastic stops the water reaching the soil, so the leaves droop.

items.stem: Which two parts of a plant take in things from outside the plant?
options: The stem and the flowers
The roots and the leaves
The flowers and the fruits
The stem and the roots

explain.why: The stem carries things and the flowers make seeds. Neither takes in water or air.
These help the plant to make seeds, not to take in things for food.
The roots take in water but the stem does not take in anything from outside.

solution: The roots take in water and mineral salts from the soil.
The leaves take in air (carbon dioxide) to make food.

figure.alt: A potted plant in line art.

items.stem: Look at the picture of the potted plant. Which row matches each part with its job?
options: A: makes food; B: makes seeds; C: carries water; D: takes in water
A: makes seeds; B: takes in water; C: makes food; D: carries water
A: makes seeds; B: makes food; C: carries water; D: takes in water
A: takes in water; B: carries water; C: makes seeds; D: makes food

explain.why: Part A is the flower, which makes seeds. Part B is the leaf, which makes food.
Leaves do not take in water from the soil. Roots do that and stems carry it.
Each job here is given to the wrong part.

solution: A is the flower, B a leaf, C the stem and D the roots.
Flower: seeds. Leaf: food. Stem: carries water. Roots: take in water.

figure.alt: A potted plant drawn in line art with its flower, a broad leaf, a stem and roots shown under the soil, with four marked positions.

items.stem: A gardener sprays water on the leaves of a potted plant every day but never waters the soil. After two weeks the plant is weak. Which is the best reason?
options: Leaves make food only when they are dry
The roots take in most of a plant's water
The stem cannot carry water from the leaves
Water on the leaves stops light from reaching them

explain.why: Leaves make food using light and air. They do not need to be dry to do it.
The stem carries water up from the roots. It does not need to carry water down from the leaves.
A little water on the leaves does not stop them from making food.

solution: Plants take in most water through their roots.
With dry soil the roots cannot take in enough water, so the plant becomes weak.

figure.alt: A potted plant in line art.

items.stem: The table shows the parts that four plants have. Which plant has what it needs to take in water, hold up its leaves and make food?
options: P
Q
R
S

explain.why: Plant Q has no leaves, so it cannot make food.
Plant R has no roots, so it cannot take in water from the soil.
Plant S has no stem, so it cannot hold up its leaves or carry water up to them.

solution: Taking in water needs roots, holding up leaves needs a stem and making food needs leaves.
Only plant P has all three.

items.stem: The table shows the parts that four plants have. Which plant has roots and leaves but no part to carry water between them?
options: P
Q
S
R

explain.why: Plant P has a stem, so water can travel from its roots to its leaves.
Plant Q has roots and a stem but no leaves, so it has no leaves for the water to reach.
Plant R has a stem and leaves but no roots, so it has no roots to take water in.

solution: Water travels up the stem from the roots to the leaves.
Only plant S has both roots and leaves but no stem.

items.stem: A bean seed has just started to grow. The first part to come out grows down into the soil before any leaves open. How does this part help the young plant?
options: It makes food for the plant
It takes in light for the leaves
It carries food to the flower
It holds the plant and takes in water

explain.why: Food is made in the leaves, and there are no leaves yet.
This part is in the soil. It does not take in light.
A young bean plant has no flower yet, and this part does not do this job.

solution: The first part to grow down is the root.
It takes in water and holds the young plant firmly in the soil.

figure.alt: A young bean seedling in line art.

items.stem: A florist keeps cut roses in a vase of water. Which part of each rose lets the water travel up to the flower?
options: The stem
The thorns
The petals
The roots

explain.why: Thorns do not carry water.
Petals are at the top. They do not carry water up.
Cut roses have no roots.

solution: The stem carries water up to the other parts.

items.stem: We eat lettuce in a salad. Which part of the lettuce plant are we mostly eating?
options: The roots
The flowers
The seeds
The leaves

explain.why: Roots are under the soil. We do not eat them in lettuce.
Lettuce is eaten before it flowers.
We do not eat the seeds of lettuce.

solution: The green, leafy part of lettuce is its leaves.

items.stem: A farmer picks off all the flowers of a tomato plant before they can form fruits. Which job of the plant part is stopped?
options: Taking in water from the soil
Holding the plant up
Making seeds for new plants
Making food for the plant

explain.why: This is the job of the roots.
This is the job of the stem.
This is mainly the job of the leaves.

solution: Flowers make the fruits and seeds.

items.stem: The roots of a tree spread out wide under the soil. How does this help the tree?
options: It helps the tree make food from sunlight
It holds the tree firmly and takes in more water
It carries food up to the leaves
It helps the tree catch more sunlight

explain.why: There is no sunlight under the soil. Leaves make food.
Roots do not carry food up to the leaves.
Leaves catch the sunlight.

solution: Wide roots anchor the tree and reach more water.

items.stem: A gardener cuts all the leaves off a plant but leaves its stem and roots. After some weeks the plant is weaker. Why?
options: It cannot make food without its leaves
Its roots cannot take in any water at all
Its stem can no longer stand up
It has too much food stored in its leaves

explain.why: The roots still take in water.
The stem still holds up the plant.
The leaves were cut off, so they store nothing.

solution: Leaves make food, so without them the plant becomes weak.

items.stem: The table shows three plants kept in the same place. Which two plants should be compared to find out if leaves are needed to keep a plant healthy?
options: P and R
Q and R
P only
P and Q

explain.why: P and R differ in their roots, not their leaves.
Q and R differ in both roots and leaves.
One plant cannot be compared with itself.

solution: P and Q differ only in the leaves.
